title: Clock and Calendar
shortDescription: Angles between hands, coinciding/opposite hands, faulty clocks, odd days and finding the day of any date.
genZNote: Clocks and calendars look like trivia but they're pure formulas. Learn 5.5 and 'odd days' and the whole chapter collapses.

sections.heading: Clock Formulas
bullets: Minute hand moves 6° per minute; hour hand 0.5° per minute; relative speed 5.5° per minute.
Angle between hands at H hours M minutes = |30H − 5.5M| (take 360° minus it if more than 180° for the smaller angle).
In every 12 hours the hands coincide 11 times, are opposite 11 times and are at right angles 22 times (44 times in a day for right angle).
Mirror image of a clock time: subtract the time from 11:60 (or 12:00 if exactly on the hour).
Slow/fast clock: compare with true time; total gain or loss = rate × time elapsed.

sections.heading: Calendar and Odd Days
sections.body: Odd days = remaining days after removing complete weeks. Leap years: divisible by 4; century years only if divisible by 400. Month odd days (ordinary year): Jan 3, Feb 0, Mar 3, Apr 2, May 3, Jun 2, Jul 3, Aug 3, Sep 2, Oct 3, Nov 2, Dec 3. Day code: Sun 0, Mon 1, Tue 2, Wed 3, Thu 4, Fri 5, Sat 6.

sections.heading: Worked Ideas
bullets: If 24 Nov 2026 is Tuesday, 1 Dec 2026 is Tuesday + 7 days = Tuesday; 1 Jan 2027 is 31 days later = +3 → Friday.
Same calendar repeats after 6, 11 or 5 years etc. depending on leap-year position (e.g. 2015 and 2026 are identical).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Clock problems use hand speeds (6° and 0.5° per minute) and calendar problems use odd days to find days of the week.
keyFacts: Leap century year needs divisibility by 400.

commonTraps: Do not forget to reduce angles above 180°.

sources.name: Standard competitive-exam reasoning reference (R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning)
